#6483. The Best New Restaurants in America in 2026

The year’s top restaurant debuts give us infinite reasons to dine out right now

These are the 15 new restaurants that best captured the year in dining. Our team of editors and scouts traveled across the country, drawing on years of experience to build the 2026 winners list.

What we found remarkable: the quiet confidence of a chef who’s mastered Hungarian food in Pittsburgh; a fresh revamp of family-style Italian dining in Philadelphia grounded in the original restaurant’s 1950s roots; a cozy tribute to Southern cuisine in Denver that still manages to feel cool. What they have in common: a sincere commitment to making diners feel at home. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

“You went to Kansas City for sushi?” I was asked more than once — with some derision — after returning from Missouri, so I can only imagine the uphill battle chef Peter Hoang faces at Akoya Omakase. Hoang isn’t easily daunted. He’s so committed to sourcing, he often personally drives to the airport to pick up the fish hand-selected by his two private buyers in Tokyo 26 hours after placing his order.

At Akoya, the fish quality is unassailable; the rice seasoned with precision. But Hoang consistently finds ways to complement Akoya’s sashimi and nigiri with unexpected accents. Smoky juvenile king mackerel gets a hit of acid and sweetness from pineapple chutney. Truffle, notorious for being overwhelming on just about anything, manifests in pate form alongside dashi and kelp salt to highlight delicate hirame. The miso-butter-accented crab nigiri (a steal at $6) calls to mind decadently dipping crab legs in drawn butter. While affordable for omakase, $165 is still a commitment: Akoya diners have the option to test the waters with a la carte offerings and lunch specials in a warm and unpretentious restaurant. Befitting the Midwestern stereotype, the personable chefs, who chat freely with those seated across the bar, are eager to answer questions. Even tables in the dining room chime in.

Hoang, who worked in his father’s mid-2000s sushi restaurant before heading to bigger markets like New York and Chicago, is excited to be part of his hometown’s emerging Japanese dining scene — one that’s increasingly drawing national attention thanks to ambitious restaurants like Anjin izakaya and promising newcomers like day-to-night Tian Tea House/Moon Bar. Kansas City just might develop a reputation for cuisine beyond barbecue. — MF

Assuming new ownership of beloved, old restaurants can be a risk, but South Philly local Joey Baldino has the formula down: Keep the trappings, dial in the food. After taking over his family’s private Palizzi Social Club and retaining its members-only allure, Baldino bought Bomb Bomb Bar, which first opened in 1951, and reopened it last year. The bar’s lore precedes it: A rival business bombed it twice, immortalized by the large neon sign of two cartoonish bombs. Some reboots feel ironic, but not this one; the payphone by the door, the swordfish on the wall, and even the endearingly gruff servers feel like they’ve been there forever. It’s proof that classic Philly and modern culinary destination Philly can coexist.

In the front room, locals analyze Eagles games, and you might hear children playing in the street. In the back dining room, the procession of seafood here, priced at $65 per person, feels like a steal in this era of rising prices. The meat for the lobster Française has been removed from its shell, battered and fried, placed onto a buttery sauce, and then crowned with its shell once more. The crispy calamari gets enlivened with twangy cherry peppers. But it’s the overall dining experience that’s unbeatable: The restaurant hasn’t reinvented the wheel, but as the Beach Boys play and you sip a pepperoncini martini while watching your server pour hot fudge onto a sundae, you remember (perhaps while still wearing a bib) that complete novelty isn’t always necessary. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Cassis is big in every sense. The nearly 200-seat dining room of the Milwaukee restaurant is an immaculately designed jewel box of gleaming tile, cozy banquettes, and antique mirrors, and even on a Wednesday night, it’s packed and roaring, with a towering, glowing bar at the center of the action. The latest project from Kyle and Meghan Knall, the couple behind nearby acclaimed bistro Birch, channels the conviviality and polish of a classic, old-world French brasserie while remaining distinctly Midwestern in spirit. It’s an all-day restaurant with both heart and panache.

Kyle Knall’s cooking roots itself in French tradition without feeling stodgy or like Parisian cosplay. Instead, it takes cues from his farm-to-table approach at Birch: Classical technique provides a framework for showing off Wisconsin ingredients with playfulness, vividness, and attention to detail. Oeuf mayo gets a jolt from intensely herbaceous, bright green aioli; ravioli Dauphiné pairs almost sugary-sweet summer corn with buttery Wisconsin-made Pleasant Ridge Reserve cheese; and an understated, frill-free but deeply umami foie gras eclair transforms one of French cuisine’s richest ingredients into an almost weightless bite.

At a moment when ambitious dining often means intimate tasting-menu counters and an air of exclusivity, Cassis makes a case that dinner can still feel like a real night out on the town. The cooking has an eagerness to please that succeeds. Within its walls, you’re offered an increasingly rare pleasure: a space where you’re invited to settle in, linger, order another bottle of wine, and maybe even have a friendly chat with the table next to you. Cassis could exist — and surely thrive — in New York or Las Vegas, but it’s more exciting in Milwaukee, where its scale and ambition feel like a vote of confidence in the city itself. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor, Eater

In 2026, the Midwest has proven a formidable destination for dining, with restaurants from Cleveland to Milwaukee leaning into what makes the region’s food special. Creepies in Chicago embodies this movement: A nonsensical (if memorable) name belies a thoughtful restaurant destination from chefs David and Anna Posey. The refreshing space feels contemporary, but with cottage-esque touches — geometric patterns dot the furniture, cartoonish artwork shares space with kitchenware tchotchkes, and mini curtains hang from open shelving.

Chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski embeds French technique into dishes fiercely grounded in Chicago’s identity. Steamed mussels get kissed with classic Pernod and a fennel giardiniera that honors the city’s iconic Italian beef sandwiches. An Alsatian-leaning tarte flambe comes “tavern-style,” a nod to the square-cut pizza beloved by locals. Not every dish invokes the Great Lakes; the generous portion of gougeres may be Midwest-appropriate, but here the French classic takes a decadent turn as warm Brie seeps from the center of each choux pastry. A textbook roast chicken’s umami-laden sauce gains extra depth from liver; drag one of the restaurant’s hefty, yet impossibly crispy fries through its drippings for the best bite of the night. Save room for Anna Posey’s desserts: The savory soft-serve trend manifests as a baguette-infused concoction topped with chocolate and buttery breadcrumbs. In a year when a diner can grow weary that Everything’s a Bistro these days, Creepies proves some still offer delights and surprises. — MF

I’ve always felt a connection to Cuban cuisine, having visited the island country in my youth and eaten many pan con lechons from LA’s Porto’s Bakery in iconic Glendale. But a July meal at Emelina, which snagged a Michelin star months after opening for its ambitious, $275 Cuban tasting menu, showed me the country’s cooking in an entirely new context.

I wasn’t the only one to find it a revelation. Several older Cubans fortunate enough to nab a reservation got emotional toward the end of the meal, moved to tears as they told me they’d never had Cuban food like this before.

Located in tony West Palm Beach, this striking restaurant from chefs Osmel González and Camila Salazar draws inspiration from the former’s family history and upbringing in Cuba. After working together at world-class restaurants like Disfrutar in Spain and SingleThread in California, they partnered with Alvaro Perez-Miranda to achieve their vision. Employing lush ingredients sourced from South Florida farms in Redland and Lake Worth, the meal starts with a tender knob of fried flounder topped with caviar — a winking nod to traditional pan con minuta, a fried fish sandwich slathered with tartar sauce. A mid-course of pristine tropical fruits including mamey, lychee, and mango, arranged over creamy ricotta and dotted with Benton’s country ham, conjures a bounty one might linger over on a Cuban beach. Rabo encendido, or braised oxtail with Koshihikari rice, takes the homestyle guisado to new heights.

Cuba has a long history of home restaurants called paladares, serving personalized versions of staple dishes like arroz con pollo. Emelina represents that same opportunity to delight and enlighten, casting attention on a cuisine and culture that could have been. In balmy West Palm Beach, it thrives. — Matthew Kang, correspondent

The winding walkway into Maroon is a portal into a new dimension, a leap from the beeps and bloops of the casino floor at the Sahara Las Vegas into a thrumming dining room, dimly lit and streaked with red-orange accents. Chef Kwame Onwuachi, who most recently earned acclaim at Tatiana in New York City and Dōgon in Washington, D.C., has become a beacon of African diasporic dishes in the middle of the Mojave Desert.

Onwuachi is building something approachable yet grounded in technique. The name Maroon comes from 17th- and 18th-century enslaved people who escaped and established mountain communities in Jamaica; the kitchen centers African and Caribbean flavors rooted in their foodways. Consider the artful array of bluefin tuna belly chunks, hamachi, and braised octopus, swimming in a tangy broth pool and best enjoyed spooned onto fried saltine crackers, that gets an intense but brief spice hit from Scotch bonnet peppers. Luxurious, palm-sized oxtail patties and jerk mushroom earn a dash of caviar and grated truffle, a maximalist garnish on the typically humble dish. Grilled butterflied shrimp brushed with achiote sofrito recall pescado zarandeado, while sweet white grape chow chow brings a puckery kick. The blackened jerk chicken, its juiciness sealed in with a crust of aromatic spices, might be the finest in the U.S.; oxtail fried rice could moonlight as Caribbean bibimbap, with saucy deboned beef and fork-tender stewed chicken on an assemblage of julienned peppers and peas. Yes, there is steak, but go for the seared, bone-in pork chop instead for its sweet glaze.

Maroon engages you with sensory brilliance and familiar yet indelible flavors, like a catchy song that gets better with each listen. In a different city, it might feel overwrought, but here in Las Vegas, it matches the city’s frenetic energy and lands like a satisfying opus. — MK

Maydan Market opened in 2025 as a collaborative restaurant space and marketplace home to a few different Los Angeles-born businesses; in essence, it functions as one super-incubator for some of the best food you can find in the city. Diners bounce around to try a pozole flight and pescadillas (sofrito-fried fish nested in supple blue corn tortillas) at Maléna, from the family behind the beloved Tamales Elena; a crisp, UFO-sized, asiento-painted tlayuda from Lugya’h, from Los Angeles legend Poncho’s Tlayudas; and chile-sauce-slicked gai tod from Golden Mountain Chicken (formerly Yhing Yhang), from the intrepid team behind Thai restaurant Holy Basil. They will certainly stop to perch at the rotating Club 104 stall, which has hosted Black-owned businesses such as Melnificent Wingz and Caribbean diasporic pop-up Rubie, as well as Palestinian home restaurant Mid East Eats. On their way out, they may circle the storefront simply named Sook to eye wines, spices, and woven goods sourced from the Levant.

This is not to mention the market’s anchor restaurants: the Lebanese-influenced Maydan and Compass Rose, respectable D.C. transplants from prolific restaurateur Rose Previte, who, alongside her team, curated the market with the knockout lineup of Indigenous vendors. Maydan Market feels boldly like one whole; people rarely come for a single hyped stall. The point, in effect, is the crawl. In a year marked by ongoing, unrelenting, nationwide ICE raids targeting Black and brown immigrants, the fact that the market centers Indigenous Mexican-owned businesses, allowing their owners the space and sovereignty to reach a wider stage and audience, speaks loudly. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

Take the former location of Portland’s — if not North America’s — most famous Northern Thai restaurant, combine it with the city’s most prolific and highly decorated Thai chef and restaurateur in Akkapong “Earl” Ninsom, and pepper in an elite local bar manager — co-owner Eric Nelson. Mix it all together, and you get OK Chicken & Khao Soi. Those familiar with its predecessor, Pok Pok, will find the space uncannily similar: a covered patio and downstairs service at a small bar, upstairs seating at oilcloth-wrapped tables. Now customers order on paper tabs. It’s casual and intimate, with just the right level of noise to feel like you stumbled into a really good dinner party.

OK Chicken’s menu leans into the flavors of Chiang Mai, starting with crispy chicken wings and two styles of khao soi — one with chicken and another richly prepared with beef. Plates of smoky nam prik makheua (eggplant dip) come with crisp and waxy long beans, green cabbage leaves, and cucumber. A memorable dish of yum moo yang — tender grilled pork shoulder tossed with snappish chunks of celery stalk and leaves as well as sliced onion — relaxes in a funky fish sauce with Thai chiles that sneakily build in your system until your lips hum. An herbal tea slushie refreshes even when mixed with a shot of infused Scotch. Close the meal with longan sticky rice speckled with perilla seeds, showered with crispy coconut and bathed in salted coconut milk that balances the sweetness of the pale lychee fruit and tangy mango ice cream on top. Each bite or sip at OK Chicken is surprising and pleasurable in equal measure. — Brenna Houck, dining editorial manager

In kitchens across the country, chefs have been happily marrying Japanese and Mexican foodways: Both cuisines have a reverence for local grains, honor highly specific seafood preparations, and play on savory, acidic flavors. Ramen Del Barrio blossomed from this shared cultural language — a Japanese Mexican izakaya centering ramen.

Chef and owner Chris Krinsky deftly laces together these threads for dishes such as creamy carnitas tonkotsu with two types of pork, confit buche and belly, as well as a chewy tangle of fresh noodles — made in partnership with Austin chef Gary Wu — using flour from a local mill. A honeycomb tripe and hominy-studded pozole tonkotsu comes rojo- or verde-style, while the mole tsukemen gets paired with thick whole wheat noodles and carnitas for dipping into rich, hearty mole. Tuna tostada, served on top of a sheet of origami paper, packs a zesty punch thanks to a dried shrimp and morita chile aioli, chicharrones furikake, eel sauce, and salsa macha. The yaki-tacos — hefty yakitori skewers served on top of corn tortillas — use smoky pulpo and vegetarian-friendly mushrooms accented with pepitas.

This isn’t fusion for fusion’s sake. Krinsky was born in Maine, grew up in Mexico, and worked at Japanese restaurants throughout most of his career. He started his ramen journey cooking out of his garage and then opened a food court stand, for which he won an Eater Award in 2023. Somehow, his menu tastes better now that he has his own dedicated space where he hand-layered wood panels along the wall and lined the ceiling with sushi mats. A small television in the dining room blasts Spanish-dubbed anime. Ramen Del Barrio 2.0 feels wholly like a loving expression of his culinary fascinations and his commitment to honoring both traditions. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

In an unmarked space in San Francisco’s Nob Hill, chef Patrick Gabon and partner Celine Wuu quietly rewrote the playbook on fine dining with Restaurant Naides. Filipino food has not historically held a footing in the Bay Area’s higher-end echelons, but Naides’s dishes make a powerful claim that the cuisine deserves its place there. Gabon deploys the sour, salty, and sweet flavors of the Philippines with subtle tenacity: The saline funk of bagoong, or fermented salted shrimp, takes on new dimension in Gabon’s hands, where the condiment gets mellowed into a creamy sauce that acts as foil to tender slices of chayote, crisp duck cracklings, and the burst of caviar. His approach to the mouth-puckering sourness of sinigang invigorates the Philippines’ national dish by pouring dry-aged beef broth over meticulously sliced abalone and scallions. These plates manage to retain the soul of the food but in new forms; they don’t placate the audience, asking them instead to reconsider their fundamental notions of fine dining and how Filipino food presented in this way may upend them.

Wuu’s beverage program has become a force of its own. It’s not often that a nonalcoholic pairing manages to outshine a traditional wine program, but Wuu keenly matches the bold flavors of each dish. A drink mixing the flavors of green mango with rooibos and habañero cordial complements the salty punch of bagoong at one turn, while coconut water, osmanthus, and rose vinegar offer a gentle start with the opening snacks, composed of Gabon’s takes on lumpia, okoy, and puto. “As you age and you grow, you tend to go deeper in your roots: ‘How can I make something so traditional the best it can be?’” Wuu told me earlier this year. Naides has answered that question with every meal since. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF

It’s tricky to pin down what exactly Rougarou is. It’s a restaurant, certainly, serving modern Southern food in the historic Five Points neighborhood in Denver. It also has a ripping bar program, late-night hours, live music on the patio, and a casual roguish charm. Inside an understated brick building on a flyby street, the dining room is full of personality, dim and moody, all hard surfaces that bounce around the fun clatter of spirited groups throughout the dinner hour.

The menu conveys the right balance of accessibility and intrigue: The ubiquitous tomato stone fruit salad gets a curry-inflected jolt of vinaigrette and a crunch of coconut benne granola. Charred zucchini is doused in smoked cheddar sauce and scattered with bits of country ham. Fried catfish sits on a pond of fermented hot and sour sauce, with pickled chiles that lash the tongue at first and Sichuan peppercorns that leave you gently tingling. And the signature Chicken on a Stick is a lovingly updated homage to a legendary gas station restaurant in Oxford, Mississippi.

While the food feels approachable, the cocktails are high-concept and assertive, leaning on tropical ingredients but pushing for wilder edges, like green banana, oversteeped oolong, and Haitian clairin, pungent and unctuous with fusel oils. A second visit, late at night, revealed a laid-back restaurant-industry hangout at the bar instead of the celebratory din I found earlier. Much like its namesake monster, Rougarou can shape-shift to host a group dinner, a date night, a jam session, or a beguiling nightcap. It’s the kind of restaurant that invites returns, and a great fit for this moment in restaurant culture. — Ben Mesirow, travel editor

D.C. hospitality veterans Jon Sybert and Jill Tyler took a risk when they converted Adams Morgan’s Michelin-starred favorite Tail Up Goat into Rye Bunny, a restaurant that straddles the line between upscale and casual. Appetizers start at $15 and entree prices go up to $40, and instead of table service, diners line up to order at a counter. In the end, both the owners and D.C. diners have seen a payoff. Sybert’s dishes are inventive yet comforting, with Aleppo honey-covered fried chicken served alongside delicately stacked anchovy and quince jam toasts built on thin slices of milk bread. Everything is still seasonal and sourced from nearby farms, but those high-grade ingredients are easier to afford now that the restaurant has been able to cut down on the number of staff by 20 percent. While D.C. diners are not crazy about queuing, the nightly line out the door has sustained for more than six months and become an unexpected way to meet neighbors. A server brings over a drink menu as you wait, so you can catch up with friends and sip on a Slovenian orange wine before you sit down.

Rye Bunny encompasses the simple joy of a neighborhood restaurant that’s an equally excellent destination for a weekday date night or a special occasion, and it represents a larger shift in our dining landscape that might save these mid-price-range restaurants as margins get thinner. — Emily Venezky, social media manager

When So. Fox opened in Atlanta’s Virginia-Highland neighborhood in July, chef Myles Moody and sommelier Rachael Pack had an instant hit, bringing new energy to that pocket of the city. But a successful restaurant often belies monumental effort behind the scenes. So. Fox’s signature dish — a whole roasted chicken — is only available to five lucky tables per night and regularly sells out before the second seating. Much like a great restaurant takes time to build, the simple bird takes days for its mustard brine to infuse, and the result is stunning: a glistening interior and exquisitely crispy skin.

So. Fox commands an insatiable demand for a table topped with that prized poultry, herby rabbit dumplings, and Carolina Gold rice. Snagging a spot at the welcoming bar or at the curved, floating table near the entry, which helps capture overflow crowds, is equally competitive. The space that formerly housed a burger joint (and before that, an auto repair shop) has been transformed into a bright, perennially packed dining room with grand windows, offering an optimal view of North Highland Avenue.

Short for Southern Fox, an American indigenous grape varietal, So. Fox showcases Pack’s longtime knowledge of natural, low-intervention, biodynamic, and Old World producers, many of whom she knows personally. Pack and Atlanta-born Moody first met while working at New York’s Michelin-starred Aska, and returned south to open Kinship Butcher & Sundry in 2021, which resides next door. This isn’t just farm-to-table; it’s produce from their own Ormewood Park farm, highlighted in grilled beef with Vidalia onions and braised leeks, and at the end of summer, in sugar snap peas with chives and farmer cheese.

It’s seasonal Southern fare that feels current and relevant, with a refreshingly casual approach — and people can’t help but show up for it. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater LA

Somssi, from Ahris Kim and chef Daniel Gronert, is one of the clearest examples in New York of a restaurant that goes all-in on personal history, rather than focusing on the broader food culture of any one country or a region.

Korea-born Kim, who ran operations at Atomix, lived in Indonesia and the Philippines before moving to Wisconsin with her family. Gronert, who has German roots and spent time as a pitmaster in South Carolina, cooked across restaurants in Atomix’s parent company. Those influences show up in dishes like the caviar-crowned Potato Potato Potato, a crispy-soft tater tot simulacrum nested on miso hollandaise; ox tongue grilled and glazed with tare, a kaleidoscope of textures; and pork schnitzel presented like shrimp toast (it works).

With the team’s fine dining pedigree, Somssi sets a high bar for hospitality, yet it’s still casual: The room is designed to feel like a home, and the menu nods to places Kim and Gronert have lived.

The bar extends that expertise. Christian Gray’s cocktails include well-made minis, which the bartenders are game to explain to curious drinkers. Sommelier (and Punch contributor) Jenny Eagleton’s list of wines and sakes leans toward lesser-known areas. The duo and their staff reward handing your night over to them, whether you’re there with a group or alone with a Kindle.

Personal touches carry through the space in gloriously analog fashion. Lace curtains on the door spell out the restaurant’s name in embroidery, and handprints line the bathroom wall, left by the broader constellation of people who helped build Somssi into the singular restaurant it is today. — NC

Sunday is a very good night to be at Titusz. That’s Schnitzel Sonntag — when the Pittsburgh restaurant, clad in warm wood and gem-toned ceramic tile, offers an irresistible special at an even more irresistible price: a 4-ounce veal cutlet, breaded and fried in lard, for $13. The golden brown slab comes with a single lemon cheek on the plate and nothing else. It takes confidence to serve a dish so simply: Chef and owner Csilla Thackray gained hers in some of the city’s top restaurant kitchens. She named Titusz after her great-grandfather, and his portrait hangs by the first-floor bar. Her own name comes from her Budapest-born grandmother, who raised the chef on her cooking.

Call it grandmacore if you want to peg Titusz to a national trend, but the menu is modern, Austrian, Hungarian, and distinctly Thackray’s. Here, meggyleves, the Magyar sour-cherry soup, gets an electrifying swirl of paprika oil. The chef has made charring an art: You will want to pick up the bowl and drink every drop of charred leek and sauerkraut broth beneath her buoyant kaspressknödel (cheese dumplings). The Maillard reaction pays off again in the savory brown butter drizzled over a dessert of aranygaluska (think walnut monkey bread), served warm on a puddle of peach creme anglaise. Thackray’s husband — Sean Rosenkrans, another veteran of Pittsburgh’s restaurant scene — has built a stunning list of wines from Central Europe, as well as cocktails fluent in that idiom — a slug of herbal Unicum here, a toasty hint of caraway there. Everything makes profound and reassuring sense together. The decision to spend money at a restaurant might feel fraught right now; the choices at Titusz never do. — Beth Kracklauer, dining editorial manager

#6482. The 8 Best Battery Packs Keep Your Gadgets Going

Top off your phone, tablet, laptop, or any other gadget without dropping everything to sit by an outlet.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It’s 2026, and everyone should have a portable battery pack in their bag, backpack, purse, or jacket pocket. We all keep at least a couple of battery-powered gadgets on us every day, including a phone, a pair of headphones or earbuds, and maybe a smartwatch. And that’s before we get into the stuff we bring to and from work every day, like laptops, tablets, handheld game consoles, and e-readers. Your battery pack is like a security blanket for your tech. It allows you to go through your day knowing that you will always have access to all your devices—even if they run out of power, you have the ability to charge them up on the spot. As a tech reporter, I never leave home without one.

And, conveniently, it doesn’t cost much to add one of these EDC tech essentials to your arsenal. Though large packs with the juice to fully recharge your laptop can get a bit pricey, you can get a pocket-sized pack to top off your phone throughout the day from a reliable brand for as little as $30 to $40. We’ve been testing these gadgets for years and have some thoughts on which ones are worthy of a spot in your bag or your pocket.

I’ve carried a battery pack on me every day for more than a decade, going back to the early 2010s, when most gadgets had modest capacities and needed at least one extra charge to get through the day. While batteries have improved, both in our devices and the battery packs, I always have one handy and am usually testing a new one or two in search of a new favorite.

For this guide, I pored over product listings and sifted through specs to find the packs with the newest features and best “estimated” performance, then spent weeks with each selection as my backup power source on the go. Whether you’re a creative pro who keeps a whole tech arsenal on hand at all times or just someone who travels a lot and needs to make sure their phone is always on, there are options on this list that will fit into your life.

The ReelCharge ReelPro 200W is the perfect ready-for-anything charger. Furnished with a 140W USB-C charging cable, plus two additional ports, this 27,000mAh laptop charger can keep all of your EDC tech powered up about as well as plugging directly into an outlet.

For reference, 140W of charging output on a single device is very fast. In 2026, most laptop charging cables can’t hit that speed. So forget about worrying whether or not your battery pack can actually charge your laptop: Now you may find yourself wishing your normal power brick could keep up.

Though not quite as impressive, it’s worth noting that 27,000 mAh is about as large a capacity as you can expect to see from a battery pack: FAA regulations ban batteries larger than 100 watt-hours, and this cuts close to that limit. There are plenty of other laptop chargers that meet the restriction, but this one packs it into a relatively compact form factor.

Not everyone loves having built-in cables in their power banks, but the feature is a must in my book. It saves time and lets you charge devices (and the pack) without worrying about whether you have an extra cable handy.

I also love that it has a built-in color screen, which lets you monitor its charging level, the power input or output of its ports, and all-around battery health. Like the onboard cable, this feature is a must in the mid-2020s and far better than the LED indicator lights of older battery packs.

The Anker Zolo offers ample 20,000-mAh battery capacity, stellar charging speeds, and abundant connectivity features that are on par with our top pick, another Anker battery. But this one is extremely cheap—less than $50. It doesn’t have the charging capacity to support high-end laptops like a MacBook Pro, but it should work wonders with just about anything else.

Having a pair of integrated USB-C cables whose braided covers match its exterior (in black, white, blue, and pink) makes the Zolo look more upmarket than the price suggests, as does the accessory’s digital display. It doesn’t show as much information as the screens on Anker’s top packs, but it is still a nice touch and rare at this price.

Anker also offers a lower-priced version of the Zolo with only one USB-C cable, which is perfect if you’re singularly focused on charging your phone.

At under $25, this highly portable pack from Baseus is the cheapest pack I’ve used and am confident recommending. With a maximum power output of 22.5 watts, the Baseus EnerFill can juice up a modern smartphone to around 50 percent in about half an hour. Its charging speed lags behind our other picks, but that's a fair trade-off, given the price.

Light and easy is the name of the game, here: It weighs just over 7 ounces and connects to devices via a built-in USB-C cable and a pair of additional ports. It even has a little flourish in the form of a digital display that gives you a more precise look at battery level than the usual pip-based indicator. Throw in a two-year warranty, and this is an incredible bargain.

The Anker Nano is, as the name implies, designed to be ultraportable. As you can see, Anker knows how to make a battery pack, and this one comes with many of the design flourishes I love in the best overall pick, including a retractable USB-C cable and a color display.

The difference here is that this is pocket-sized and made to support smaller gear. In this case, though, “smaller” really just means everything but the most heavy-duty tech. With a 10,000-mAh battery pack and a maximum power output of 45 watts, it can rapidly power up any phone and tablet. It can also extend the screen time of compact notebooks like the MacBook Air. It’s not suitable for MacBook Pros, however.

This is a solid compromise for folks who want a lot of charging power but need a smaller charger, or want to keep their budget under $60.

In a crowded field of magnetic battery packs designed to snap to the back of an iPhone or a top-shelf Android phone, I’ve come to rely on the Sharge Icemag 3 because of its original design, fast wireless speed, and some unique special features.

It supports Qi 2.2, the latest wireless charging standard, which can deliver up to 25-watt output. When you plug in its integrated USB-C cable, that speeds up to 35 watts, which is enough to top off some lightweight laptops.Beyond the basics, the Icemag 3 has some interesting extra features, including a sturdy kickstand, and an onboard cooling fan to help it maintain consistent charging speeds. Most magnetic battery packs want to fade into the background, but the Icemag 3 has the look and the feature-set to stand out and make a strong impression.

If you’re going backpacking and you need a battery pack that can take a little bit of punishment, we like Nestout’s rugged offering. Its shockproof exterior and IP67 rating for water and dust resistance mean it’s ready for long camping trips where it might spend a little time in the dirt. The ports also feature screw caps with tight seals, providing complete protection between charges.

With a 15,000-mAh battery capacity, three charging ports, and a maximum power output of 32 watts, this version of the battery pack offers a fine balance between speed and versatility. Smaller Nestout power banks with capacities of 10,000 and 5,000 mAh are also available. All battery packs are compatible with additional accessories, including a solar charger and an attachable USB light.

The Powerstation Mini is the most compact pack I’d consider using regularly and truly lives up to its “mini” moniker. It's just a tad larger than a tube of lipstick and slips easily into the smallest pocket in your jeans or a clutch purse. And thanks to a sleek aluminum shell, it doesn’t look like a tech accessory when not in use.

There is a price for its minuscule footprint, though—slower charging speed. Still, this is more than fine for juicing up your phone or a pair of earbuds in a pinch.

The Anker Prime sets itself apart from other laptop-grade battery packs with its retractable wall plug. It may sound like overkill, but having one unlocks higher power output to charge or power large laptops and other, less portable devices.

I like the battery pack’s sleek design, with a built-in color screen that displays vital information about the charging process and its remaining capacity. As a final throw-in, it comes with a very nice braided USB-C cable.

Needless to say, there are a lot of battery packs out there, and for every one that I’ve recommended here today, my fellow editors and I have tested many alternatives. Honestly, as long as you’re sticking with brands with a reputation for quality, the difference between our picks and the next best thing is pretty small: Either they cost a bit more than the competition for a similar offering, or charge at a slightly slower rate. In a couple of cases, they’re legitimately just as good, but fill a niche that not many people need. Here are a few highlights from our most recent tests:The latest run of battery packs from battery pack founding father Mophie includes the Powerstation Plus Mini 5K and, the Powerstation Plus 10K, as well as the Powerstation Plus Signature Series Mini 5K and Powerstation Plus 10K. In attempting to make battery packs for every price point, the brand has stretched its offerings too thin. The standard Powerstation Plus packs are genuine bargains at $30 and $40, but lack competitive charging speeds and features. The Powerstation Signature Series packs have faster rates (though not the fastest we’ve tested), and braided cables, which make them more durable. If the Signature Series packs were priced like the Standard Series, they’d be shoo-ins for the list. As is, they lack a superlative spec on which to hang their hats.

We’ve also tested a new raft of battery packs from Ecoflow, a brand you may be familiar with if you’ve read our guide to solar generators. The most recent options from the brand’s “Rapid” power bank series all feature 45W fast-charging, which is faster than average for a small to mid-size pack. Senior Commerce Editor Mike Epstein says the best of the bunch, the Rapid 20K, is pretty remarkable: You get a lot of power and fast charging for less than $50. The pack is a bit large, though: It’ll fit in your pocket, but maybe not comfortably. Ecoflow also makes a number of novel options, like the Rapid 10K 3-in-1 charger, which can do double duty as both wall charger and power bank. Like the Rapid 20K, it’s an interesting pack. Either one of these could earn a spot on our list one of these days, because their performance and price are very appealing, but we’re keeping them here for now because they fill a more specialized niche than any of our current picks.Lastly, we should highlight the Nimble Sharepower, an interesting 10,000 mAh power bank that can split apart into two 5,000 mAh packs, so two people can charge devices independently. Again, it’s a niche pick aimed at parents looking to keep their kids’ iPad charged without sacrificing their own backup power. At $80, it’s a bit pricey for what it is. (You can buy two 5,000 mAh packs for less.) But if you can see it being useful, this is a unique choice that could be a lifesaver for the person, in the right situation.

Capacity is the be-all, end-all of any battery (or battery pack), as it determines how much power your device can store. Typically measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), the higher your battery pack’s capacity is, the more power it has to distribute to your devices throughout the day.

Keep in mind, though, that a larger capacity almost always means a larger, heavier, and more expensive battery pack. As you can see from our picks, there are good reasons to buy different packs with different capacities based on what you plan to charge, and how you plan to carry it.

For most people, I recommend looking for a pack around 10,000 mAh, which should be portable enough to fit in your pocket and have enough juice to charge your phone a couple of times, or a smaller device four times or more. This should be enough to get your essential EDC gadgets through a day of extremely heavy use (like when you’re traveling), or a long weekend off-grid.

If you are carrying a laptop, a digital camera, or a large number of devices that all need charging from time to time, you should probably scale up to a larger “laptop charger” battery pack that can hit 20,000 mAh or more. The limit here is usually 25,000 to 28,000, as most manufacturers want to keep the battery under the FAA’s 100-watt-hour battery capacity limit for passenger airliners. (If you’re looking for something bigger that doesn’t need to fly, consider our guide to portable power stations.)

Capacity is the obvious and highly publicized metric for battery packs, but it is often power output that separates the good chargers from the bad ones. Output, measured in watts (w), tells you how fast the battery pack can charge your devices. The actual speed will also depend on the output supported by the device it’s charging. But a faster battery pack will be helpful, especially with larger, more expensive gear.

For most people, I recommend getting a battery pack that delivers at least 45 watts of power from a single output. That’s enough to rapidly charge phones and ultraportable laptops like the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air. Faster options are few and far between, and you’ll only need them for large devices like a MacBook Pro or a gaming laptop.

That said, many battery packs don’t hit that speed, and I wouldn’t immediately dismiss them out of hand. The smaller your pack’s capacity, the less likely you’ll need a fast-charging pack. Try to look for 30 watts in a compact power bank, but even less than that is okay for pocket-sized options, especially if it’s a slim, wireless charging pack that attaches directly to a phone.

It’s important to note that using a battery pack to charge multiple devices often slows down charging across each device. Depending on the construction, the pack’s maximum output can be spread across one or many ports. While shopping, keep an eye on the output of each port. And when you’re charging, keep in mind that you should only charge one device at a time when time is of the essence.

Unless the power bank you’re eyeing is super tiny like the Mophie I recommend above, look for a device with an integrated USB-C cable. Having the wire built in is super convenient. You can use it to charge devices and replenish the power bank itself. More than one built-in cable is preferable for larger power banks.

Additional USB-C outputs are also mandatory for a battery pack, unless it’s super tiny—again like the Mophie Powerstation Mini already mentioned. An old-school USB-A port is also great to have, just in case, especially on larger power banks.

#6481. Asteroid Mining Will Crash the Platinum Market, But That’s Good News for Earth

Science fiction authors have been dreaming of robotic spacecraft harvesting fortunes from asteroids for decades. Humanity is slowly getting closer to that reality. But if you ask asteroid mining skeptics, they will usually ask one specific question - what happens to the prices of all those rare materials once someone actually brings them back? A pair of system dynamicists from MIT directly tackled that question with a new paper titled Will AstroForge Collapse the PGM Market?

Platinum Group Metals, or PGMs, are absolutely critical to modern industry. Two of the most commonly used are platinum and palladium, which are critical components in everything from automotive catalytic converters (hence when thereâs a raft of people stealing them) to hydrogen fuel cells. However, these materials are exceptionally hard to come by - on Earth at least. More than 80% of the known planetary reserves are locked in deep-shaft mines located in South Africa and Russia.

Their absurd prices (tens of millions of dollars a ton) are based at least in part on how difficult they are to extract. Even at the Russian and South African mines, they are only able to glean a few grams of material per ton of rock. In the process, they require ventilation, cooling, and heavy machinery, as well as actual laborers down deep mine shafts. That sounds exactly like the kind of industry that is ripe for disruption - at least if there is another source of the raw material.

Fraser talks about whether we will mine asteroids.

Luckily, there is. Metallic (M-type) asteroids are the leftover metallic cores of protoplanets, and carry concentrations of PGMs dozens of times higher than even the richest mines on Earth. A single kilometer-wide space rock of this type holds more PGMs than humans have extracted throughout all recorded history. No wonder these particular materials have been the focus on asteroid mining efforts for decades.

AstroForge, a start-up based in California, is one of a second-round of asteroid mining start-ups that are focusing specifically on returning PGMs to Earthâs market. Instead of multi-billion dollar asteroid mining craft, they specialize in small, agile probes that cost only a few million dollars each to launch. The value of what they return, though, is much higher.

Their architecture involves latching on to the metallic asteroid using magnets. High power lasers then vaporize the asteroidâs crust, and an onboard refinery separates the PGM gas from the less valuable nickel and iron that makes up the majority of the asteroidâs bulk. After the PGMs have been refined, they are blasted back to Earth in a heat-shielded return capsule, ready to be brought to market on Earth itself. That way, the company only ships high value material rather than processing minerals that donât have as much value back down on Earth.

Isaac Arthur is much more bullish on our eventual ability to mine asteroids, as he discusses in this video. Credit - Isaac Arthur YouTube Channel

Understanding how this would affect the terrestrial market is the focus of the paper, and researchers Robert Nachtrieb and Steven Smith built a dynamic computer simulation tracking what they believe will happen to the PGM market over a 20 year period following the first successful return of a chunk of material from an asteroid. According to their model, there will be a dramatic, two-phase transition.

The first phase can be thought of as a âspace gold rushâ. The prices for PGMs have been held artificially high by lack of supply - a classic problem in traditional economics. Once the supplied amount changes - such as when new sources come online, the price begins to fall as the supply line of the classic âXâ graph moves to the right. But it doesnât happen overnight. At the start, space-based metals will be able to be sold at normal prices, allowing the asteroid mining companies to enjoy astronomical profit margins.

Those profit margins will, at least in theory, drive plenty of additional private investment, which in turn will be used to expand the production capacity of the space-based options. According to the paper, this will drive a cycle where industry profits will skyrocket to eight times what they currently are during this first phase. Thatâs enough to make whoever successfully send material back first fabulously wealthy.

But eventually, the second act will begin - what the authors describe as equilibrium collapse. Global supply of PGMs will far exceed original terrestrial amounts, and the market prices will start falling dramatically. High cost mines, such as those operating in North America, will be the first casualties. The Russian and South African behemoths, though, will not be far behind, as they will be unable to maintain a profit with the lower price caused by the increased supply. Over the course of fifteen years, terrestrial mining supplies will be completely replaced by space-mined ones, and market prices will drop by over 75%.

That might sound like terrible news for the terrestrial mining industry - and to put it bluntly, it is. But itâs great news for everyone else. Cheaper PGMs mean less expensive hydrogen electrolyzers, and therefore a less expensive transition to the âgreen economyâ for the rest of the world. In addition, space-based mining does not have all the acid mine drainage, arsenic pollution, and hazardous labor in deep tunnels that are required to get PGMs out of the ground on Earth.

Which all sounds like a much better future for humanity more generally. The problem is the engineering challenges to get to that point. Astroforge has had a few high-profile failures during its development cycle so far. But thatâs the case with any fast-moving ânew spaceâ company. It is undeniably getting closer to making this future world of green tech provided by space rocks a reality. And, if they do manage to do so, everyone involved should become extremely wealthy in a span of less than two decades.

#6480. The Ice Giants' Magnetic Fields are Very Strange Compared to Earth's

Most planets appear to have magnetic fields, even if they're only weak, remnant fields. Earth has a strong field generated by its internal geodynamo. The other rocky planets have magnetic fields of varying strengths, with the possible exception of Venus. The outer gas planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, all have strong dynamos.

But the magnetic fields generated by the ice giants Uranus and Neptune have some strange properties.

Earth's molten core and internal convection generate its magnetic fields. But the ice giants' magnetic fields are likely generated by fluids that are electrically conductive. These are water, ammonia, and methane ices under extreme pressure and temperatures that alter them and turn them into ionic and superionic phases. Not only is their electrical conductivity at play, but so is convection and the planets' rotations.

But beyond what generates them, they also have other differences. Earth's magnetic field has well-defined north and south poles that drift a little over time, and even flip every couple of hundred thousand years or so. But Voyager 2 showed us how different Uranus and Neptune are. Their fields are in disarray compared to Earth's. They're tilted and multi-peaked.

Uranus' magnetic field doesn't originate in its center, and is tilted almost 60 degrees from its axis of rotation. It's overall geometry is strange, and the magnetic field across its surface is asymmetrical in strength.

Neptune's magnetic field is similarly strange, but weaker. Like Uranus' it's tilted from its rotational axis, by about 47 degrees. It's also offset from the planet's physical center like Uranus'.

The most critical difference between the magnetic fields of Earth and those of Uranus and Neptune is that the fields around the ice giants experience shorter-term variability. In short, they're a weird mess.

While planetary scientists know that these fields are generated inside the planets, they've had to make some guesses as to why they're so strange. New research in Nature Communications Physics has made some progress understanding the pair of ice giants and their strange magnetic fields. It's titled "Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune," and the lead author is Chi Yan. Yan is a research associate at the University of Texax Jackson School of Geosciences.

"Uranus and Neptune exhibit magnetic fields that are non-dipolar and non-axisymmetric, unlike those of any other known planet," the researchers write. "These fields are generated by fluid motions in electrically conducting planetary interiors via dynamo action, offering a window into otherwise inaccessible deep processes."

As we often say at Universe Today, understanding the oddballs and outliers in a group of objects sheds light on how processes operate across the broader group they're a part of. This is true of the ice giants and their magnetic fields. "Understanding why Uranus and Neptune have such unusual magnetic fields provides critical insight into dynamo processes across planets and stars," the authors explain.

This work is based on modelled dynamos that are controlled by interior composition and temperature. They assumed that electrical conductivity increases with depth. The authors say they "produce large-scale magnetic features consistent with the observed fields of Uranus and Neptune..."

This schematic shows the different interior layouts used in the models. a through c show radially variable electrical conductivity profiles for dynamo models with convective shell geometries. d through f show the associated shell geometry for each of a through c. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

âDeep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high,â lead author Yan said in a press release. âUnder these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.â

Voyager 2 gave us our only good close-up look at Uranus and Neptune. It likely caught those fields in a snapshot in time, and the model shows both planets' magnetic fields could shift and change markedly in only decades. The fields are most likely configured much differently than when Voyager 2 visited. This is much different than on Earth, where the magnetic north pole drifts between about 5 and 60 km per year, or about one degree every few decades.

"These non-dipolar dynamos exhibit substantial temporal variation, although the rate fluctuates and can be transiently slow," the authors write. They explain that changes in both intensity and orientation are a possibility in the decades since Voyager 2 flew past Uranus and Neptune, "though the extent of any such variation remains poorly constrained observationally as each planet has been measured in situ only once."

âEarthâs magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years,â said Yan. âOur models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.â

This figure compares observations of Uranus' and Neptune's surface magnetic fields with the fields from models. The figure "demonstrates that the most Uranus-like snapshot from Model 6 (panel c) and the most Neptune-like snapshot from Model 11 (panel d) can change substantially on decadal timescales, with their close morphological resemblance to the respective observed fields (panels a and b) deteriorating markedly after 32 years (panels e and f)," the authors explain. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

"We demonstrate that dynamo models incorporating an electrical conductivity that increases with depth can promote non-dipolar, non-axisymmetric magnetic fields," the authors write, including the M1 peak observed at Uranus and Neptune.

The M1 peak is an important, maybe the most important part, of Voyager 2's magnetic field observations. M=1 represents the lop-sided parts of a magnetic field. On Earth and other planets like Jupiter and Saturn, the magnetic field's power is dominated by symmetric or M=0 components. So for those planets, the M-1 components are at least an order of magnitude weaker than their M-0 components.

But that's not true on Uranus and Neptune. They show a stark contrast. They both have a very strong M-1 peak, the part that represents asymmetric fields. This means that they have dipoles, quadrupoles, and octupoles that are messy and skewed from the axis of rotation.

"Despite current observational and computational limitations, our results indicate that ice-giant-like dynamos can, in some intervals, undergo substantial magnetic field variations on decadal timescales that, if confirmed by future in situ or auroral measurements, could have significant impacts on the surrounding planetary magnetospheres," the authors write.

The JWST has observed the ice giant aurorae and the charged particles involved. These particles respond to the magnetic fields, and those observations could confirm if the magnetic fields have indeed shifted since Voyager 2 visited. Researchers are still working on those observations.

The image on the left is an enhanced-color image of Neptune from NASAâs Hubble Space Telescope. On the right, that image is combined with data from NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope. The cyan splotches are auroral activity captured with the JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec). Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Heidi Hammel (AURA), Henrik Melin (Northumbria University), Leigh Fletcher (University of Leicester), Stefanie Milam (NASA-GSFC)

âWe are busy working on whatâs contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an important stepping stone,â said Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign.

The researchers will combine the JWST data with their models and data from Voyager 2 and take their results as far as they can to try to determine the state of the magnetic fields today. But they're up against some limitations, limitations that can only be lifted by another mission to the ice giants.

There are no firm plans for a mission to the ice giants, but there are concepts. One is NASA's Uranus Orbiter & Probe that would study the planet and its moons, and even send a probe into Uranus' atmosphere. The Neptune Odyssey is another NASA concept. It would also consist of an orbiter and an atmospheric probe. The science community has recognized the importance of these missions, but they're just concepts at this point.

This research may extend to the issue of habitability, though probably only tangentially. Uranus' four major moons could all potentially have subsurface oceans under icy covers, though this is far from confirmed. If they do, then Uranus' magnetic field and related radiation belts could affect these bodies of water, their longevity, and their potential habitability.

#6478. The Best Frame TVs Bring a Discreet, Tasteful Look to Your Living Room

These alternative screen designs feature matte, anti-glare displays that make static art look just as good as your favorite movie.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Unlike conventional TVs, which display a black screen when powered off, frame TVs display museum-quality artwork, family photos, and other media. With customizable bezels in various materials and colors, they look like picture frames and blend better with your home’s aesthetic.

While early frame TVs were all style and no substance, the technology behind these displays has evolved significantly. Today’s models feature matte screens that reduce glare, brightness sensors that automatically adjust to ambient lighting, and advanced display technologies that match the best 4K TVs on the market.

When shopping for a frame TV, factors like screen size, display quality, and style play a role just as they would with the best gaming TVs. However, frame TVs introduce additional considerations. Some premium models offer interchangeable bezels in various materials, while installation is a bit more challenging. They may also include free access to curated galleries, though some require monthly subscriptions. Below, we’ll dive into all the features to consider when searching for a solid frame TV, along with a few recommended picks.

For this roundup, I established clear criteria that each TV had to meet to qualify as a true “frame TV.” First and foremost, they had to have an elevated design beyond the traditional black rectangle—a design that can blend into your existing décor. Second, each model needed a dedicated art mode with specialized screen technology—like anti-glare—that minimizes reflections. Lastly, I considered options with some form of customization, including interchangeable bezels and curated art libraries. Samsung’s The Frame earns our top recommendation for effectively pioneering this category, offering a beautiful design, matte display, and extensive art collection. That said, each model in this roundup offers unique advantages. Whether you’re looking for a premium art display, a design statement, or a more budget-friendly option, our selections cater to various preferences and price ranges.

Samsung’s The Frame made a splash when it debuted in 2017, creating a TV that perfectly disguised itself as a piece of art. A few generations later, the TV looks even better and has the technology to match. The 2025 model brings years of refinement, featuring a QLED 4K display, an anti-reflective matte coating, and quantum dot technology that delivers vibrant colors and deep contrast.

The Frame’s anti-glare coating gives the TV a canvas-like appearance, so you can place it in a bright room without the picture washing out. When the art mode is activated, the matte finish helps diffuse ambient light, creating the illusion that you’re standing before an actual painting in a gallery. Samsung’s adaptive brightness sensor further enhances this effect by automatically adjusting the display’s brightness to match the room’s lighting conditions throughout the day.

Additionally, the TV features a built-in motion sensor that detects when you enter or leave the room, automatically turning its art mode on/off to save power. The Frame further helps save energy by lowering its refresh rate from 120 Hz to 60 Hz when art mode is activated. To help eliminate cable clutter, The Frame comes with an external hub that houses all the TV’s ports and connections, so you can hide everything from view.

Samsung's Art Store, which provides access to more than 2,000 curated works of art, requires a monthly subscription. Meanwhile, the TV's customizable bezels are sold separately and typically range from $100 to $200, depending on size and material. This can add to the overall cost of the TV, which already comes at a premium.

TCL’s frame TV line, Nxtvision, brings the art display concept to a more accessible price point while still offering advanced features such as a 4K QLED display, a high refresh rate, and next-generation gaming capabilities. At just 1.1 inches deep, the Nxtvision TV is incredibly thin, and it comes with a mount so it sits flush against the wall.

Like other options on this list, it features an anti-glare screen, which creates a convincing paper-like look, maintaining the illusion of physical artwork. The TV’s processor can also optimize color, contrast, and clarity, ensuring you get the best picture quality no matter what’s being displayed.

In addition to a curated gallery featuring various styles and periods, there’s an AI art capability that generates custom artwork from prompts. Additionally, you can display your personal photo gallery, giving you a huge picture frame for your favorite memories. The only drawback is that the Nxtvision comes with its own proprietary mount, so it’s not VESA-compatible, which may limit your mounting options.

If you’re in the market for another value pick that doesn’t scream “technology” when not in use, the Hisense CanvasTV is a mid-range lifestyle TV with an art mode that showcases Renaissance paintings, family photos, and more. Its matte display reduces reflections and gives artwork more depth and texture, so pictures look like actual paintings.

Additionally, the ultra-slim wall mount lets you hang it flush against the wall for that coveted gallery look. The magnetic frame system (teak comes standard) also lets you easily change the look of the CanvasTV to match your décor. Just note that it only comes in just two sizes, 55 and 65 inches, limiting placement options.

The CanvasTV doesn’t sacrifice performance for aesthetics, delivering an excellent picture with its 4K QLED display. Gamers will also appreciate the 144 Hz refresh rate and Auto Low Latency Mode, ensuring smooth gameplay without screen tearing or motion blur. Together, the combination of design and features makes the CanvasTV an excellent value.

The LG G5 isn’t necessarily a gallery TV like Samsung’s The Frame, but it features a slim design with a barely noticeable bezel, plus a gallery mode for showcasing artwork and photos. For these reasons, and others, including best-in-class picture quality, we believe this pick is a good entry point for those who want to upgrade their current model to a hybrid lifestyle TV.

On the G5’s OLED display, images look stunning thanks to perfect blacks, infinite contrast, and vibrant colors. It also offers better brightness—a major weakness of OLED—with some clever engineering that helps the screen stay vivid. However, as good as the OLED display is, it can still appear slightly washed out in bright ambient light, which may influence where you place it in your room.

While it doesn’t offer customizable bezels like The Frame, the LG G5’s minimalist aesthetic naturally complements modern interiors without sticking out like a sore thumb. Without a stand, the TV is just 1 inch thick, creating a sleek, floating appearance that doesn’t protrude from your wall.

Beyond its aesthetics, this pick also offers excellent functionality. Its four HDMI 2.1 ports allow you to enjoy gaming at 4K resolution with a smooth 120 Hz refresh rate. Dolby Vision support ensures that movies look their best, and Filmmaker Mode helps preserve the director’s original vision, providing the optimal viewing experience.

As frame TVs have grown in popularity, their size range has increased, too. When Samsung’s The Frame launched in 2017, it was available in only a few sizes. But now, the TV is available in sizes ranging from 32 inches to 85 inches. Frame TVs from other manufacturers also come in a variety of sizes, allowing you to get the option that best fits in your space.

When you’re shopping for a frame TV, I recommend resisting the urge to go for the largest size you can afford. Instead, think about how far you’ll be sitting from the screen. A huge TV in a small room can actually make viewing uncomfortable, because you’ll need to constantly move your eyes across the screen to take in all the action—it’s like sitting too close to a theater screen.

On the flip side, a TV that’s too small can force you to squint to make out details. Finding the sweet spot is crucial, especially with frame TVs designed to blend seamlessly with your décor. That sweet spot will vary depending on the available space, décor, etc., but generally, you should measure the area where you plan to place the TV before purchasing it.

Whether you’re shopping for a premium TV or something more affordable, there are different display technologies you should know about, including QLED and OLED. In the TV space, QLED is a common option among top manufacturers. This technology employs quantum dots to enhance color vibrancy and brightness, making it perfect for viewing art or pictures throughout the day.

Meanwhile, OLED is still widely regarded as the best display technology because of its ability to deliver true blacks and infinite contrast. Each individual pixel is self-emitting, meaning it can turn completely off when displaying black, providing a stunning viewing experience for high-contrast content.

While OLED is making its way into some high-end frame TV options, it offers lower peak brightness than QLED. This can make content appear less vibrant in well-lit rooms, so it's worth considering if you’d like to display bright content on your TV.

While frame TVs are generally wall-mounted, they come in a few installation styles. Wall mounting creates the illusion that your TV is a picture frame (hence the name), allowing it to hide in plain sight.

Most manufacturers include the appropriate mounting hardware, but the customizable bezels that allow you to match your TV’s frame to your décor are typically sold separately. This extra hardware generally comes in different wood tones and colors to best match your taste.

While a frame TV mostly serves as a decorative piece, there are a few extra features that sweeten the deal. Most models include dedicated art modes featuring curated galleries with thousands of classic and contemporary artworks.

However, if you want to access the full galleries with artwork from the world’s leading museums and artists, you may have to pay a subscription fee. For example, Samsung’s The Frame requires a subscription to its art store to access more than 2,000 iconic images

Frame TVs also incorporate auto-brightness features that use built-in sensors to detect your room’s ambient light. These sensors automatically adjust the screen brightness, similar to how smartphones adapt their displays between indoor and outdoor environments.

Many models also include motion sensors that detect when someone enters the room, automatically activating the display to show artwork without requiring you to turn the TV on manually. Additionally, frame TVs typically incorporate anti-glare technology that reduces reflections, creating a more authentic, canvas-like appearance.

A DNA analysis has confirmed that a Nazca infant who lived in southern Peru 1,600 years ago had a rare congenital condition called trisomy 13.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Peru have discovered the skeleton of an infant with a rare birth defect that left only one central eye socket in the child's skull. DNA analysis of the remains confirmed a chromosomal abnormality caused the deadly condition in the infant over 1,600 years ago, according to a new study.

"We cannot really say how long this individual survived," study co-author Lars Fehren-Schmitz, an anthropologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told Live Science in an email. But "the burial of this infant suggests that the Nasca treated this individual in death like most other infants."

The skeleton of this female infant was discovered alongside a second one inside a ceramic urn at the archaeological site of Jauranga in Peru's Palpa Valley, where numerous geoglyphs known as the Nazca Lines have been found. Archaeologists uncovered several dozen other burials dated to the Middle Nazca (also spelled Nasca) period (A.D. 325 to 440) at the site, but one of the co-buried infants had an extremely rare condition, researchers wrote in a study published Monday (Nov. 9) in the journal PNAS.

The infant had a very small skull and a single eye socket in the middle of her face, along with other developmental issues of the cranial bones. These traits match modern clinical descriptions of cyclopia, a lethal condition that occurs when the front part of a fetus's brain fails to divide into left and right hemispheres.

This condition can also cause alterations in the nasal structures, resulting in a missing nose or a tube-like nose above the single eye.

A medical illustration from 1891 of two infants with cyclopia.

"The cause of the malformation was present at fertilization, but manifestation occurs around the fourth to fifth week in utero [in the womb], when the frontal lobe of the brain has to divide," study first author Elsa Tomasto-Cagigao, an archaeologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told Live Science in an email.

Cyclopia is a rare condition, occurring in about 1 out of every 100,000 births. To learn more about the infant's short life, the researchers sequenced her genome. (DNA suggested the infant carried two X chromosomes, typical of a female.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team detected an extra copy of chromosome 13, meaning the infant had a genetic condition called trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome. It's known to be a major chromosomal cause of cyclopia; that said, only a small percentage of trisomy 13 cases involve cyclopia.

While trisomy 13 is associated with advanced maternal age, it is not clear whether that was the case for this infant, Fehren-Schmitz said.

"This condition has been documented in historic and modern anatomical collections, but to my knowledge this is the first archaeological example of this developmental abnormality," Siân Halcrow, a bioarchaeologist at Durham University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

The researchers' estimate of the infant's age at death suggests she may have survived for several weeks or months after birth, Halcrow pointed out. "This raises important questions about how infants with profound congenital differences were cared for and treated in past societies," she said.

The infant was buried in a ceramic urn, the researchers noted in the study, which was a common burial method in the Nazca period, along with a second female infant who had no skeletal abnormalities. "The baby with cyclopia was at the bottom of the jar, while the other baby was on top. Nevertheless, it appears that they were interred in a single event," Tomasto-Cagigao said. The genetic analysis showed that the two infants did not have the same mother.

A burial of two infants in one urn is unusual for this culture, the researchers said, but there is not enough archaeological evidence to conclude that the infant with cyclopia was given a different type of burial.

"The fact that the individual was buried with a 'healthy' individual in a regular cemetery, without any special grave goods, suggests that, to some extent, the individual was not treated differently in death, even though it had such a rare condition," Fehren-Schmitz said. "It was neither 'excluded' because of it nor treated in a 'special' way."

In ancient Andean societies, some people with disabilities took on special societal roles, such as ones associated with religious practices. "If that reflects Nasca society as a whole, we can't say based on one case," Fehren-Schmitz said, "but it does reflect the community this infant was part of, even if only briefly."

Tomasto-Cagigao, E., Reindel, M., Isla Cuadrado, J., Lund Valle, M., Kassadjikova, K., Harkins, K., Fehren-Schmitz, L. (2026). A Nasca-period perinatal burial reveals cyclopia associated with trisomy 13 in southern Peru. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.2625042123
